common_name: Disco Marigold (AAS-Winning Single-Flowered French Marigold Series)

planting.note: Direct sow after frost, or start indoors a few weeks early for earlier bloom; Disco is an early, free-flowering single (not double) French marigold series bred for uniform bedding displays.

directions: Direct sow or transplant into well-drained, average soil in full sun. Disco is a landmark All-America Selections-winning French marigold series notable for its single, flat, open-faced flowers in gold, orange, red, and yellow bicolor tones, a departure from the fully double pompon form typical of most bedding marigolds, giving plants a daisy-like look that shows off dark contrasting basal blotches on many selections. Plants form compact, uniform mounds that flower quickly and heavily from seed and hold up well to summer rain and heat. Deadheading keeps the display going through the season, and like other marigolds the pungent foliage is largely ignored by deer and rabbits, making it useful as a border planting around vegetable beds.

common_name: Antigua Marigold (AAS-Winning Compact Dwarf American Marigold Series)

planting.note: Start indoors a few weeks before last frost or direct sow once soil has warmed; Antigua is a dwarf, early-flowering American marigold series bred to bring the large double blooms of tall African marigolds onto a compact bedding-sized plant.

directions: Start indoors or direct sow into well-drained, average soil in full sun. Antigua is an All-America Selections-winning American (African) marigold series bred by PanAmerican Seed to combine the huge, fully double, carnation-like pompon blooms of tall African marigolds with a compact, uniform 10-14 inch bedding habit, in gold, orange, primrose, and yellow selections. It flowers earlier and more heavily than taller African types and holds up well through summer heat with minimal care. Deadhead spent flowers to prolong bloom, and expect the pungent foliage to be largely avoided by deer and rabbits, making it a useful edging plant around vegetable gardens.

common_name: Inca Marigold (AAS-Winning Dwarf Early-Flowering American Marigold Series)

planting.note: Start indoors a few weeks before last frost or direct sow once soil has warmed; Inca is an early, weather-tolerant, dwarf American marigold series widely grown from seed for bedding and containers.

directions: Start indoors or direct sow into well-drained, average soil in full sun. Inca is one of the most widely grown American marigold series, an All-America Selections winner bred for large, fully double 3-4 inch pompon blooms in gold, orange, and yellow on compact, well-branched plants that flower notably earlier from seed than older tall African marigold types and tolerate rain and heat without collapsing. The later-introduced Inca II series added further color range and improved weather tolerance. Deadhead to keep flowers coming through summer; the strongly scented foliage is generally left alone by deer and rabbits, and the series is a popular companion planting around tomatoes and other vegetables.
sources: Cornell University Flower Bulb Research Program — Annual Marigolds

common_name: Aurora Marigold (AAS-Winning Early-Flowering French Marigold Series)

planting.note: Direct sow after frost, or start indoors a few weeks early for earlier bloom; Aurora is an early-flowering, fully double French marigold series bred for uniform, compact bedding plants.

directions: Direct sow or transplant into well-drained, average soil in full sun. Aurora is an All-America Selections-winning French marigold series bred for very early, heavy flowering from seed on tidy, compact, uniform mounds, producing fully double crested blooms in gold, red, and yellow-and-mahogany bicolor tones. It holds its neat habit and continues flowering through summer heat with only routine deadheading. As with other marigolds, the pungent foliage is generally avoided by deer and rabbits, making it a useful edging and companion plant around vegetable beds.

common_name: Red Gem Marigold (Deep Red-Orange Signet Marigold)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in full sun to partial shade; in zone 9 plant February-April for spring and September for fall. Like other signet marigolds, Red Gem blooms continuously without deadheading and tolerates heat and humidity better than French or African types.

directions: Sow directly on the soil surface or lightly covered in any well-drained soil; Red Gem is the deep red-orange member of the Gem signet marigold series (Tagetes tenuifolia), alongside Lemon Gem and Tangerine Gem, forming a mounded plant of fine, ferny, lemon-scented foliage smothered continuously in small single flowers from late spring through fall. The flowers and young leaves are edible, with a sharp, citrusy, slightly spicy flavor good as a garnish in salads and desserts. The strongly aromatic foliage deters whiteflies, aphids, and nematodes when interplanted with vegetables, and plants are drought-tolerant once established, reseeding modestly in warm-winter gardens.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Edible Flower Guide
